claims.summary: A model build validates syntax and references. It is useful for structural changes but does not establish the invoice amount or end-to-end inventory effects.
The testing unit distinguishes Scalar Value from Row Count. A deterministic expected total tests the calculation rather than merely the existence of one row.
Row Count is appropriate when cardinality is the requirement. The supplied defect preserves row count while changing the amount, so this does not address it.

Integration tests exercise sequences across procedures, triggers and tables. An isolated, known-state database lets this test observe cross-object effects that a single-value unit test does not cover.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Re-read the actual testing-level, test-condition and integration sections for this new generation. A Row Count condition measures cardinality, Scalar Value measures a result cell, and integration tests exercise interacting objects against a deployed target. These distinctions support two complementary tests, without asserting that SQL unit tests run without a database.

The captured build section checks model references and target-platform syntax, then emits the dacpac. It supplies structural validation, not execution of invoice arithmetic or inventory transitions. I exclude its overly broad repeat-deployment-idempotence statement from this candidate's evidence.

choiceReviews.rationale: The already-green model build has not executed either business operation. Repeating that structural gate cannot reveal the wrong scalar or inconsistent end state; it remains useful for syntax/reference defects, a different class of failure.
For a deterministic fixture, a Scalar Value condition compares the invoice-total cell to its expected amount. This detects the stated defect even though the result still contains exactly one row.

Substituting another cardinality check for value checking cannot distinguish two one-row results containing different amounts. A Row Count condition is legitimate when quantity is the contract, but is insufficient for this specified scalar-value defect.

Executing the related procedures and trigger in a deployed isolated database, then asserting order and inventory state, exercises the cross-object workflow that the training assigns to integration testing. This addresses the second risk rather than duplicating the scalar test.
